source.title: Algorithmic progress in language models
source.authors: Anson Ho; Tamay Besiroglu; Ege Erdil; David Owen; Robi Rahman; Zifan Carl Guo; David Atkinson; Neil Thompson; J. Sevilla

page_placements.theme: Algorithmic progress changes compute requirements over time

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present; some equations and table formatting have minor extraction artifacts.
record.tranche_reason: The paper fits scaling-law-inspired models to historical language-model evaluations and tests their fit and robustness, rather than reproducing the original controlled scaling experiments.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own fitted loss exponents and model-fit comparisons. Its algorithmic-progress doubling times, transformer estimates, and cited results about other studies are not rows for the claim versions unless they directly test a version. Appendix B computes implications of Kaplan and Chinchilla scaling laws, but does not empirically test whether the compute-optimal parameter/token split follows a stable power of compute.
record.test_reason: The study uses the Chinchilla loss form mainly as a tool to estimate algorithmic progress. It still reports its own fitted N and D exponents on about 231 historical models (WT103, WT2, PTB). It compares them with Kaplan and Hoffmann and explains the gap by the fitted compute range, which bears on V1 and V7. The power-law form is imposed rather than tested against alternatives, so the evidence is indirect.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors find compute to reach fixed perplexity halved about every 8 months (95% CI around 5–14). Compute scaling contributed more to gains than algorithms (60–95% by Shapley). The transformer was worth about 3–46x in compute. They caution that the data are noisy and that parameter estimates should not guide compute-optimal scaling.
record.recipe_differences: The study fits augmented scaling-law models to a heterogeneous historical dataset of evaluations across years and benchmarks; it does not perform the original controlled training sweeps.
record.method_sensitivity: The fitted results depend on model specification and on how training data is defined. The paper reports similar compute-doubling estimates under several data definitions, but different central estimates when unknown epoch counts are dropped. It also reports that scaling-law predictions diverge outside much of its observed compute range.

fits_no_version.finding: Compute needed to reach fixed perplexity halves about every 8.4 months (95% CI 4.5–14.3). The transformer gives a 7.2x compute-equivalent gain.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Pre-training algorithmic progress in LMs halves the compute needed for fixed loss roughly every 8 months.

record.problems: The authors report noisy and uneven benchmark data, sparse pre-2017 data, missing parameter counts and evaluation details, and wide confidence intervals. Their comparisons are observational and use heterogeneous evaluations. They also caution that their parameter estimates are not reliable enough to strongly inform compute-optimal scaling.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted under the 60-row limit. Results concerning historical algorithmic-progress doubling times and transformer compute-equivalent gains were left out because they do not measure the loss-scaling or compute-optimal-allocation versions in the claim.

untested.parts: No controlled sweep varying N, D or compute with the other quantities non-bottlenecking; the power-law form is assumed, not tested against alternatives.
Not tested empirically. Appendix B only computes consequences of the published laws, and the authors say their estimates cannot inform compute-optimal scaling.

missing.what: Exponents change with the definition of training data: tokens seen gives αparam 0.135 and βdata 0.024; diminishing returns gives 0.081 and 0.036 (core: 0.068 and 0.040).
Robustness fits leave the exponents much the same. With an irreducible loss term: αparam 0.068, βdata 0.040. With the autocorrelation model: 0.076, 0.031. With the transformer model: 0.079, 0.029.
missing.locator: Appendix H Table 8; Appendix I Table 9; Appendix D Table 3

missing.what: The compute-only power law gives αcompute 0.004 and a very poor out-of-sample MSE of about 0.72. The plain Chinchilla form without a year term fits worse (MSE about 0.066) than model 7 (about 0.049).

record.verdict_notes: The scaling law serves mainly as the scaffold for estimating algorithmic progress, so its bearing on V1 and V7 is secondary and observational. R4 and R5 should be unlinked from the claim versions.

versions.untested_parts: The study uses historical benchmark evaluations and a fitted model; it does not run a controlled sweep that separately varies parameters, tokens, and compute while holding the other quantities non-bottlenecking.
The paper does not test whether laws fitted on small runs predict runs orders of magnitude larger. Its leave-one-out predictions are not reported as small-to-large extrapolations.
The paper does not empirically estimate how compute-optimal parameter and token counts grow with compute. Appendix B calculates consequences of the Kaplan and Chinchilla prescriptions.
No controlled comparison of architecture details at fixed parameter count is reported.
The analysis concerns language-model pretraining evaluations on WikiText and Penn Treebank, not other modalities or the listed alternative training regimes.
The study analyzes next-token prediction loss, not downstream task performance.

The study examines fitting choices, differing fitted exponents, and divergence between scaling-law predictions across compute ranges. It does not establish that empirical loss curves bend away from a single power law.

rows.subject: 231 language-model evaluations analyzed with model 7 (aggregate)
rows.size_stated: Aggregate of models with reported parameter counts; individual sizes vary.
rows.operation_detail: Fit an augmented scaling law to cross-entropy loss using parameter count, training dataset size, and publication year.
rows.measure: Parameter scaling exponent in the fitted loss model
rows.note: The fitted loss term varies with parameter count using this exponent. The paper says the resulting parameter and data estimates imply cross-entropy loss scales roughly as C^-1/20.
rows.check: The power-law form is imposed by the model, and loss also depends on a year term. The exponent is significantly positive but far below the originals' values, so this shows only that loss falls with N in this setting.

rows.subject: 231 language-model evaluations analyzed with model 7 (aggregate)
rows.size_stated: The analysis spans over 8 orders of magnitude of training compute; around 80% of models with known compute lie between approximately 4 × 10^17 FLOP and 10^22 FLOP.
rows.operation_detail: Compare the fitted loss-scaling relationship with prior scaling-law estimates and examine its behavior across compute ranges.

conditions.value: Most known-compute observations lie between approximately 4 × 10^17 and 10^22 FLOP

rows.measure: Cross-entropy loss scaling with training compute
rows.value: The paper says its fitted exponents suggest cross-entropy loss scales roughly as C^-1/20; it reports Kaplan et al.'s exponent as around -0.048 and Hoffmann et al.'s as around -0.3.
rows.note: The paper reports its own estimate and comparisons to prior work. It says the laws strongly diverge below around 10^18 to 10^19 FLOP and above 10^22 FLOP, while being more similar in slope between those ranges.
rows.check: For V1, read as partial: the C^-1/20 slope is implied by the fit, not measured directly. For V7 it is observed: the exponent differs from Hoffmann (~-0.3), and the authors attribute this to the fitted data range.

source_check.correct: The eligible dataset contains around 231 models; the main analysis excludes approximately 50 more by retaining at most three models per paper. The fitted exponents imply approximately C^-1/20; around 80% of models with known compute lie between approximately 4 × 10^17 and 10^22 FLOP.
source_check.locator_found: Section 2.2.2; Appendix C.1, Figure 9 and surrounding paragraphs.

rows.subject: Kaplan and Chinchilla scaling-law optima (paper's calculation)
rows.size_stated: Dense autoregressive transformer compute range from 10^19 to 10^25 FLOP
rows.operation_detail: Minimize the two published loss functions over parameter count and training data at fixed compute budgets, then compare the compute needed to match their predicted losses.

conditions.value: Kaplan et al. 2020 versus Hoffmann et al. 2022 scaling laws

rows.measure: Compute-equivalent multiplier for switching from Kaplan to Chinchilla scaling
rows.baseline: Kaplan scaling-law loss at the specified compute budget
rows.note: This is a calculation using the two laws, not an empirical test of compute-optimal parameter or token growth.
rows.check: A calculation from the two published laws, not an empirical result. It should not be a row.

rows.subject: Candidate augmented scaling-law models (aggregate comparison)
rows.size_stated: Around 90 model specifications considered in cross-validation; 15 main candidate model numbers are described.
rows.operation_detail: Compare alternative scaling-law specifications, including forms with changing scaling exponents, by leave-one-out cross-validation.
rows.measure: Out-of-sample fit of alternative scaling-law specifications
rows.baseline: Model 7 has R² around 0.91; its MSE test loss is 0.0486, compared with 0.0485 for model 10.
rows.value: The alternatives that model different scaling behavior or changing exponents also typically achieve R² between 0.88 and 0.91. Model 14 performs roughly as well as models without algorithmic progress.
rows.note: The authors select model 7 despite model 10's slightly lower MSE because model 7 uses two fewer parameters and gives a single interpretable rate. They describe exponent-only progress in model 14 as negligible.
rows.check: This is the study's own model selection among algorithmic-progress specifications. It does not measure scaling exponents' dependence on setup.

relationships.condition: Historical LM evaluations on WT103/WT2/PTB, about 4e17 to 1e22 FLOP for most data
relationships.reason: In the imposed power-law fit, loss falls with N and D with significant exponents (0.068, 0.040), with held-out R² around 0.91. The form is assumed and exponents are much smaller than the originals' (R1, R2, R3).
relationships.display_finding: The imposed power-law fit estimated significant parameter and data exponents of 0.068 and 0.040, with held-out R² around 0.91.
